title: FirstLight — API rescue sketch and operator field kit
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, operator-friendly runbook sketch for rapid containment and early diagnosis of common API degradations: hard timeouts, client 429s (rate-limited rejections), degraded streaming (slow or broken chunk delivery), and sudden elevated error rates.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood API endpoints (hosted + dedicated fleets) and runtime proxies.
- Focus on on-call actions (first 0-45 minutes), quick mitigations, and handoff notes.
- Deeper RCA and long-term fixes go into weekly postmortem.

Quick triage (first 5 minutes):
1) Verify alert origin and impact: which product route, customer, region? (Slack alert, PagerDuty, Opsgenie).
2) Check SLI dashboard (Grafana): request rate, error rate, p50/p95 latency, streaming chunk latency, rate_limiter_rejections.
3) Determine scope: global vs region vs single customer vs single model.
4) Run sampling curl to reproduce (if safe):
   curl -i -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"model":"gpt-x","input":"ping"}' --max-time 10
   - Note: do not run heavy load tests from oncall. Use single small request.

Observable signals and what they usually mean:
- Spikes in api_request_timeout_count + p95 latency rising: overloaded backend or stuck KV/cache calls (warmup/regrowth)
- rate_limiter_rejected_total rising: sudden traffic burst or misconfigured quota change.
- request_stream_chunk_latency_ms increasing: network egress or streaming buffer backlog.
- internal_5xx_ratio rising but 4xx stable: runtime bug, new deployment, model OOM, or GPU memory pressure.

Useful Prometheus queries (copy/paste):
- API error ratio (1m): sum(rate(api_request_errors_total[1m])) / sum(rate(api_request_total[1m]))
- Timeouts: sum(rate(api_request_timeout_total[5m])) by (route)
- 429s: sum(increase(api_response_status_total{code="429"}[5m])) by (route)
- Streaming chunk latency p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_stream_chunk_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- Rate limiter rejects: sum(rate(rate_limiter_rejected_total[1m])) by (policy)
- GPU memory pressure: avg_over_time(gpu_memory_used_bytes[5m]) / avg_over_time(gpu_memory_total_bytes[5m])

Tools / dashboards to open immediately:
- Grafana: "API - Overview", "Rate Limiter - Policies", "Serving Runtime - GPU/CPU", "Streaming - Chunking"
- Kibana/Logs: filter by request_id or route, time window = alert window
- Trace UI (Jaeger/tempo): sample trace of 5 failing requests
- Redis/Cache metrics dashboard

Containment playbook (by symptom)
A) Hard timeouts (client hits configured timeout or backend stops responding)
  1) Check runtime pod health and recent deploys: kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -l app=runtime -o wide | grep CrashLoop
  2) Check CPU/GPU and network egress for affected pods. If GPU pinned to high memory usage, consider evicting low-priority pods (scale down non-critical pools).
  3) If one AZ/region affected, shift traffic using routing policy to healthy region (console -> route override -> point traffic to fallback model/region).
  4) If timeouts are caused by long-running KV/cache miss storms: flush or warm caches for hot prefixes (only if safe).
  5) Short-term mitigation: increase API gate timeout at proxy layer by +2-5s for affected route (console or envoy config). Note: increases SLO breach risk; communicate immediately.
  6) If caused by a long-running evaluation job or strained disk I/O, kill the offending job/process via infra runbook.

B) Elevated client 429s (rate limiter rejections)
  1) Confirm origin: which rate-limiter policy is rejecting? Use query rate_limiter_rejected_total{policy=~".*"} and inspect policy labels.
  2) Determine if this is legitimate load spike or bug (client misbehaving sending many parallel requests). Look at recent deploys of SDKs, see linked_artifacts.
  3) If it's a known enterprise customer and we need emergency relief, increase their quota temporarily (console -> customer -> quota adjust).
  4) If global, consider relaxing the tightest policy for a short window (temp policy override) or enable graceful backoff header to clients.
  5) If cause = bug in our request fanout (duplicate requests), roll back the last deploy.
  6) Communicate: post to #sre-ops and #platform-status with what was done and ETA for resolution.

C) Degraded streaming (slow or incomplete streaming)
  1) Check streaming chunk latency histograms and network egress errors.
  2) Confirm whether degraded to all streaming clients or only some SDK versions. Filter by client or user-agent.
  3) Check connection counts and HTTP/2 stream limits on front proxy and runtime. Look for low ephemeral port exhaustion.
  4) If chunking is stalling, as a temporary workaround flip route to non-streaming (buffered) mode for affected tenant/route via console routing. This increases latency but avoids partial outputs.
  5) For broken gRPC streams: restart the front-proxy pods in a staggered manner to avoid connection storms.
  6) If caused by slow model generation (large context or expensive model), route to a smaller model variant or reduce default max_tokens for the route.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spike, validation errors, partial failures)
  1) Sample request logs, group by error message, route, model. Often a new model variant rollout or config change causes a spike.
  2) If rollout in last 30m, rollback the rollout (console -> rollouts -> rollback).
  3) If errors are internal (OOM, ModelLoadFailed), mark the model as degraded and route traffic away to fallback variant.
  4) If errors are downstream (KMS/HSM, external storage), check downstream service health and enable cached response fallback where applicable.

Decision matrix (short):
- If errors coincide with deployment -> rollback.
- If errors coincide with traffic burst -> rate limit adjustments or short-term quota increases for affected customers + slower route.
- If errors coincide with resource exhaustion on GPUs -> scale pools or drain lower priority jobs.
- If only streaming is affected -> switch to buffered/non-streaming fallback.

Command snippets (for on-call):
- Check runtime pods: kubectl -n redwood-serving get pods -l app=runtime -o wide
- Check recent deploys: kubectl -n redwood-serving rollout history deploy/runtime --revision
- Tail logs for route X: kubectl -n redwood-serving logs -l route=chat-completion -f --since=15m | grep ERROR | head -n 200
- Check rate limiter rejects: kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/prometheus 9090:9090 & open http://localhost:9090 then paste query: sum(rate(rate_limiter_rejected_total[1m])) by (policy)

Escalation & communications:
- PagerDuty escalation rules apply; if unresolved after 30 minutes and customer-visible, escalate to SRE lead and on-call product manager.
- Post an incident stub in #platform-status with: summary, impact, mitigation, ETA, contact.
- If any enterprise customer has SLA exposure, ping CS & account owner immediately.

Verification checklist (how to know we’re better):
- Error ratio drops to baseline for 10 minutes and p95 latency returns under SLO for 5 minutes
- Affected customers report back healthy (if customer-facing incident)
- No residual 429 spikes in next 30m

Short post-incident template (fill after containment):
- Incident title:
- Lead responder:
- Timeline (minute resolution): detection -> actions -> containment -> full recovery
- Root cause hypothesis (initial):
- Evidence collected (prometheus links, traces, logs):
- Actions taken (short-term mitigations):
- Follow-ups (owners + due dates):
  - Permanent fix (code/config) -> owner -> due date
  - Monitoring alert tuned -> owner -> due date
  - Customer comms / credits -> owner -> due date

Playbook caveats & operational notes (operator-to-operator):
- Avoid broad cache flushes unless confident; cache storms during warmup can spike latency. Prefer warming hot prefixes.
- Increasing proxy timeouts helps briefly but masks real root cause and may increase downstream backlog. Use sparingly.
- For streaming degradation, restarting front proxies one-by-one is safer than mass restart.
- When increasing quotas for a customer, document the change in the ticket and set an automated rollback in 30 minutes.

Short checklist for post-handoff/next shift:
- Attach sampled traces and 20 failing request logs to the incident ticket
- Note any policy changes done (timeouts, quota, route overrides) with times and who approved
- Add follow-ups to weekly SRE sync if cross-team work is required

Notes to self (open questions and TODOs for this document):
- Add exact Grafana panel links (TODO: screenshot IDs)
- Decide safe list of models to route-to as fallbacks for each critical customer
- Add scripted commands for automated temporary quota bump in console (with rollback flag)
- Document exact proxy config field names for timeout overrides (envoy -> route.timeout_ms?)

Appendix: common quick PromQL examples (human readable)
- api error rate (5m): sum(increase(api_request_errors_total[5m])) / sum(increase(api_request_total[5m]))
- per-route p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))

End of sketch.

This doc is intentionally terse and operator-focused. Use it as a pocket kit during on-call; expand into a fuller runbook with exact links and scripted runbooks in the next SRE retro.

-- Asha
